unit_name: Growth, Development & Influences Across the Lifespan
lesson_title: The Five Life Stages & Their Developmental Milestones
content_html:
Why Life Stages Matter

Health and social care professionals do not treat all individuals the same way. They use a lifespan framework — dividing human life into five distinct stages, each with its own expected pattern of growth and development. Understanding these stages helps practitioners identify what is typical for a person’s age and what might indicate a problem. When a child or adult does not reach an expected milestone, a practitioner needs to know what “on track” looks like before they can help.

Development is described across four domains, remembered using the acronym PIES — Physical, Intellectual, Emotional, and Social. These four threads run through every life stage, changing in pace and character as an individual moves from infancy to later adulthood.

Key Fact

The five life stages and their age boundaries are: infancy (0–2 years), childhood (3–10 years), adolescence (11–19 years), adulthood (20–64 years), and later adulthood (65 years and over). Exam questions that ask for age boundaries only credit these exact ranges.

Stage 1: Infancy (0–2 Years)

Infancy is the period of the most rapid development in the entire lifespan. A newborn baby is entirely dependent on their caregivers but begins building skills at an extraordinary pace. Health visitors and midwives work closely with families at this stage to monitor that development is on track.

Physical: Infants are born with primitive reflexes such as the rooting reflex and the grasp reflex. By around 12 months, most infants can sit unaided and begin to pull themselves upright. By 18–24 months many take their first independent steps. Weight typically triples in the first year.

Intellectual: Infants learn through their senses and through exploring objects. Language begins with babbling around 6 months, progresses to single recognisable words by around 12 months, and simple two-word combinations by 18–24 months.

Emotional: An infant’s most significant emotional development is forming an attachment bond with a primary caregiver — the foundation for emotional security later in life. Distress when separated from a caregiver (separation anxiety) begins around 6–8 months.

Social: Infants begin making eye contact within weeks of birth and develop social smiling by around 6 weeks. They learn to interact with familiar faces and are soothed by familiar voices. Most social interaction at this stage is with immediate family.

Stage 2: Childhood (3–10 Years)

Childhood is a period of steady physical growth alongside rapid intellectual and social development. Children in early years settings, primary schools, and community clubs are acquiring skills that will shape the rest of their development. A nursery key-worker or primary school support assistant plays an important role in observing milestones at this stage.

Physical: Gross motor skills (running, jumping, climbing) and fine motor skills (drawing, writing, cutting) continue to develop. By around age 5 most children can dress themselves and use scissors accurately. Height and weight increase steadily but more slowly than in infancy.

Intellectual: Language expands rapidly — vocabulary grows from around 200 words at age 2 to several thousand by age 7. Children learn to read, count, and solve simple problems. They move from egocentric thinking toward understanding others’ perspectives (theory of mind). Concentration spans increase as formal schooling begins.

Emotional: Children develop a clearer sense of their own identity and begin to compare themselves to peers. Self-esteem can be influenced significantly by praise or criticism from adults. Fear of failure and pride in achievement both emerge in this stage.

Social: Play becomes increasingly cooperative rather than parallel. Friendships form on the basis of shared interests. Primary socialisation (learning values and norms from family) begins to be supplemented by secondary socialisation through school and peer groups.

Stage 3: Adolescence (11–19 Years)

Adolescence spans the transition from childhood to adulthood and is characterised by dramatic physical changes (puberty) and significant shifts in how a person sees themselves. Adolescents may interact with GPs, school nurses, and youth workers during this stage.

Physical: Puberty triggers growth spurts, development of secondary sex characteristics, and changes in body composition. In girls this typically begins between ages 10–11; in boys slightly later at 11–13. By the end of adolescence physical growth is largely complete.

Intellectual: Abstract thinking and the ability to consider hypothetical situations develop. Young people can weigh up consequences, form opinions, and think critically. This supports academic achievement at GCSE and A Level and development of personal values.

Emotional: Identity formation is the central emotional task of adolescence — young people explore who they are in relation to their peers, family, culture, and aspirations. Mood fluctuations are common as hormones and social pressures combine. Self-esteem is strongly linked to peer relationships.

Social: Peer groups become more influential than family in shaping behaviour. Adolescents begin to form their first intimate relationships outside the family unit. The balance between seeking independence and still depending on caregivers is a defining social tension of this stage.

Stage 4: Adulthood (20–64 Years)

Adulthood is the longest life stage. It spans a huge range of experiences — from a 20-year-old starting their first job to a 60-year-old approaching retirement. Physical development peaks in early adulthood and then gradually begins to decline. GP practices, occupational health services, and family support workers all interact with adults across this stage.

Physical: Physical strength and fitness peak in the mid-twenties. From the thirties onwards gradual changes occur — metabolism slows, muscle mass reduces, and skin begins to show signs of ageing. For women, the menopause typically occurs between ages 45 and 55, ending the reproductive years.

Intellectual: Adults apply accumulated knowledge to complex real-world problems. Career development, managing finances, and raising children all require higher-order reasoning. Intellectual performance generally remains high throughout adulthood, though the speed of processing information may slow slightly from middle age.

Emotional: Adults form long-term intimate partnerships and close friendships. Managing the emotional demands of work, parenting, and caring responsibilities is a key feature of this stage. Life events such as bereavement, redundancy, or divorce can significantly disrupt emotional wellbeing.

Social: Social networks are typically at their widest in early and middle adulthood — work colleagues, community involvement, and family ties create a rich social world. Parenting and caregiving roles bring new social responsibilities.

Key Fact

Physical development peaks in early adulthood (mid-twenties) and gradually declines from that point. The menopause, marking the end of female reproductive capacity, typically occurs during adulthood (ages 45–55) — not in later adulthood as students often assume.

Stage 5: Later Adulthood (65 Years and Over)

Later adulthood begins at 65 and continues until death. The experiences of people in this stage vary enormously — a healthy 68-year-old runner and a 90-year-old with advanced dementia are both in “later adulthood” by the spec’s age classification. Geriatric wards, hospices, day centres, and residential care homes are all settings where practitioners support individuals at this stage.

Physical: Bone density decreases (increasing fracture risk), muscle strength reduces, and sensory abilities such as sight and hearing may decline. Immune function weakens. These changes increase the likelihood of long-term health conditions.

Intellectual: Many older adults remain cognitively active and continue acquiring new skills. However, processing speed typically slows, and some individuals experience memory loss — in its more severe forms this may indicate dementia, which increases in prevalence with age.

Emotional: Retirement can be a positive transition (freedom, leisure) or a difficult one (loss of purpose, identity). Bereavement becomes more frequent as friends and partners die. Maintaining a positive sense of self despite physical decline is a key emotional challenge.

Social: Social networks may shrink as mobility reduces and peers die. Loneliness and isolation are significant risks. However, many older adults maintain strong family ties and remain active in community groups, faith communities, and volunteering.

unit_name: Growth, Development & Influences Across the Lifespan
content_html:
Physical Development: A Story of Change

Physical development is the most visible dimension of growth — the changes a person can see and feel in their own body. It follows a broadly predictable sequence from birth through to later life, though the pace and nature of change shift dramatically between the five life stages. Health and social care professionals — from health visitors monitoring infants to nurses on geriatric wards supporting older adults — use knowledge of physical development to assess how well an individual is doing for their age.

Infancy (0–2 Years): Reflexes, Growth and First Skills

Newborn babies arrive equipped with primitive reflexes — automatic responses that help them survive. The rooting reflex turns a baby’s head toward anything that strokes its cheek, supporting feeding. The grasp reflex causes the fingers to close around anything placed in the palm. The Moro (startle) reflex throws the arms outward in response to a sudden noise or drop. These reflexes fade over the first few months as voluntary control develops.

Physical growth is fastest in infancy. A typical baby doubles its birth weight in around five months and triples it by twelve months. Height increases by roughly 25 cm in the first year alone. The brain grows rapidly too — achieving around 90% of its adult volume by age two.

Key Fact

Newborns are born with primitive reflexes (rooting, grasp, Moro) that support survival. These fade as voluntary motor control develops — a sign of healthy brain maturation. Health visitors monitor this pattern at standard checks in the first year.

Motor skills develop in a head-to-toe direction. Gross motor skills include sitting unaided (around 6 months), crawling (around 9 months), pulling to standing (around 10 months), and walking independently (around 12–18 months). Fine motor skills develop alongside — an infant progresses from a palmar grasp (using the whole hand) to a pincer grasp (thumb and forefinger) by around 9–12 months.

Childhood (3–10 Years): Growing Coordination and Self-Care

Physical growth slows and becomes more steady during childhood. Children gain roughly 5–7 cm in height and 2–3 kg in weight per year. Coordination improves significantly — by age 5 a child can typically run, hop, and kick a ball with control.

Gross motor skills in childhood include skipping, riding a bike, throwing and catching accurately. Fine motor skills develop toward controlling a pencil, using scissors, and fastening buttons and laces. These self-care skills are important markers of independence that practitioners in early years settings observe carefully. Delays in fine motor development can indicate conditions such as dyspraxia and may prompt referral to an occupational therapist.

Adolescence (11–19 Years): Puberty and the Growth Spurt

The most dramatic physical change in adolescence is puberty, driven by hormonal changes that cause rapid growth and the development of secondary sex characteristics. School nurses and GPs often provide advice and support during this transition.

In girls, puberty typically begins between ages 10–11. Changes include: breast development, widening of the hips, growth of pubic and underarm hair, the onset of menstruation (periods), and a growth spurt. Girls generally complete puberty by around age 14–16.

In boys, puberty typically begins slightly later, around ages 11–13. Changes include: growth of the testes and penis, development of pubic, facial, and body hair, voice deepening (voice “breaking”), growth of muscle mass, and a later but more prolonged growth spurt. Boys generally complete puberty by around ages 15–17.

The adolescent growth spurt means a young person may gain 8–10 cm in height per year at its peak. Body composition changes significantly: boys gain muscle mass; girls gain body fat proportionally as the body prepares for potential pregnancy. Acne is common in both sexes as sebaceous glands become more active in response to hormonal changes.

Adulthood (20–64 Years): Peak, Pregnancy and Menopause

Physical strength, cardiovascular fitness, and reaction speed all peak in the mid-twenties. This is the phase when the body performs at its optimum. From around age 30 onwards, gradual change begins: muscle mass decreases by roughly 3–5% per decade, skin elasticity reduces, and bone density begins to fall.

Pregnancy is a significant physical experience during adulthood. The body undergoes major hormonal, cardiovascular, and physical changes to support the growing foetus. Blood volume increases by around 40–50%, the uterus expands from the size of a pear to accommodate a full-term baby, and weight typically increases by 10–12 kg. Midwives and obstetricians monitor these changes through antenatal care.

The menopause typically occurs between ages 45 and 55. The ovaries stop producing oestrogen, ending menstruation and fertility. Common symptoms include hot flushes, sleep disturbance, mood changes, and reduced bone density (increasing osteoporosis risk). GPs and women’s health nurses often support women through this transition with advice on HRT (hormone replacement therapy) and lifestyle adjustments.

Key Fact

The menopause occurs during adulthood (typically ages 45–55), not later adulthood. This is a common exam error. The drop in oestrogen increases the risk of osteoporosis and can cause symptoms including hot flushes and sleep disturbance.

Later Adulthood (65+): The Ageing Process

The physical changes of later adulthood are largely the continuation and acceleration of changes that began in adulthood. However, in later adulthood they are more pronounced and more likely to affect independence and quality of life.

Musculoskeletal changes: Muscle mass declines more rapidly (sarcopenia), joints stiffen due to cartilage wear, and bone density falls — raising the risk of osteoporosis and fractures, especially hip fractures in falls. Practitioners in residential care settings manage fall prevention programmes for this reason.

Cardiovascular and respiratory changes: The heart muscle weakens slightly, blood vessels lose elasticity, and lung capacity reduces. This means older adults tire more quickly with exertion and may have reduced stamina.

Sensory changes: Sight and hearing both commonly deteriorate. Presbyopia (difficulty focusing on close objects) and age-related hearing loss (presbycusis) are very common. Opticians and audiologists play important roles in supporting people at this life stage.

Skin and appearance: Skin thins, loses moisture, and wrinkles. Hair whitens or thins. These changes are normal but can affect self-image and emotional wellbeing.

content_html:
What Is Intellectual Development?

Intellectual development, also called cognitive development, is about how the mind grows. It covers memory, concentration, reasoning, problem-solving, language acquisition, and the ability to think in abstract terms. Like physical development, cognitive development follows a broadly predictable sequence — but theorists such as Jean Piaget and Lawrence Kohlberg have given us specific frameworks to describe how thinking changes at each life stage.

In health and social care, understanding cognitive development helps practitioners communicate appropriately. A support worker in a nursery setting needs to know that a 3-year-old thinks very differently from a 10-year-old. A mental health nurse working with an older adult needs to understand what normal age-related memory change looks like — and what might indicate dementia.

Piaget’s Four Stages of Cognitive Development

Jean Piaget (1896–1980) was a Swiss psychologist who argued that children move through four distinct stages of cognitive development. Each stage represents a qualitatively different way of thinking — not just knowing more, but thinking in a fundamentally different way. Piaget called the mental frameworks through which we interpret the world schemas. As children encounter new experiences that don’t fit existing schemas, they either assimilate the new information or adapt their schemas to accommodate it.

Key Fact

Piaget’s four cognitive development stages, in order: sensorimotor (birth–2 years), pre-operational (2–7 years), concrete operational (7–11 years), formal operational (12 years+). Questions often ask you to name the stage AND describe one feature of it.

In the sensorimotor stage, infants learn about the world through their senses (sight, touch, taste, sound, smell) and through physical actions — reaching, grasping, mouthing objects. Thinking at this stage is tied entirely to what is immediately present and perceived. A key milestone Piaget identified is object permanence — the understanding that objects continue to exist even when out of sight. This typically develops at around 8–12 months. Before object permanence, an infant will not search for a toy hidden under a cloth; after it, they will.

In the pre-operational stage, children develop language rapidly and begin to use symbols (words and images) to represent objects. However, their thinking has important limitations. It is egocentric — the child cannot easily take another person’s viewpoint. A child in this stage will assume that because they can see something, everyone else can see it too. Piaget also noted that pre-operational children lack conservation — the understanding that quantity stays the same even when appearance changes. For example, a child in this stage will say there is “more water” in a tall thin glass than in a short wide one, even when told the same amount was poured.

In the concrete operational stage, children can now think logically, but only about concrete, real-world events they can observe directly — not about hypothetical or abstract situations. They master conservation, can sort objects by multiple criteria (e.g. size and colour), and understand that actions can be reversed (reversibility). Children at this stage can follow instructions in a step-by-step way and solve practical problems, making this stage important for understanding school-age learning.

In the formal operational stage, the individual can now think abstractly — about hypothetical situations, ideals, and possibilities that don’t exist in front of them. They can reason systematically (like a scientist testing a hypothesis), consider multiple viewpoints simultaneously, and form their own values and beliefs. This stage maps onto adolescence and continues into adulthood. Not all adults reach or consistently use formal operational thinking in all contexts.

Kohlberg’s Three Levels of Moral Development

Lawrence Kohlberg (1927–1987) built on Piaget’s work to describe how moral reasoning develops across the lifespan. He presented people with moral dilemmas (including the famous “Heinz dilemma”, in which a man must decide whether to steal a drug to save his wife’s life) and studied the reasons they gave for their answers, not just the answers themselves. Kohlberg identified three levels of moral development, each divided into two stages.

Key Fact

Kohlberg’s three levels of moral development are: pre-conventional (self-interest and consequences), conventional (rules, authority, social order), and post-conventional (abstract ethical principles). Most children operate at pre-conventional; most adults at conventional; a minority reach post-conventional.

Pre-Conventional Morality (Kohlberg’s first stage) is typical of young children. Moral decisions are based on self-interest: behaviour is right if it avoids punishment or gains a reward. A child at this level might say stealing is wrong because they would get into trouble — not because it harms another person.

Conventional Morality (Kohlberg’s second stage) is typical of older children, adolescents, and most adults. The individual follows rules because they value social order, the approval of others, and the expectations of family, peers, and society. Doing what is “right” means following the law, being a good friend, or meeting social expectations.

Post-Conventional Morality (Kohlberg’s third stage) involves reasoning beyond rules and social approval. The individual recognises that laws can be unjust and applies universal ethical principles (such as justice, human dignity, equality) even when they conflict with social rules. Kohlberg believed this level is reached by only a minority of adults. A health worker who challenges an unethical policy on principle is demonstrating post-conventional reasoning.

Cognitive Development in Later Adulthood

Piaget’s framework does not describe specific changes in later adulthood — his stages are complete by adolescence. However, cognitive changes do occur as people age. Processing speed typically slows, and episodic memory (recall of recent events) is often the first to decline. Acquiring new knowledge and learning new skills remains possible throughout later adulthood, though it may take longer. Maintaining mental stimulation through reading, puzzles, social interaction, and learning new activities is linked to better cognitive outcomes.

unit_name: Growth, Development & Influences Across the Lifespan
lesson_title: Social & Emotional Development — Bowlby, Ainsworth & Burke
content_html:
Social and Emotional Development Across the Lifespan

Social and emotional development describes how individuals build relationships, develop a sense of who they are, and learn to manage their feelings. It begins in the first weeks of life with the formation of an attachment bond and continues through adolescent friendships, adult partnerships, and the social challenges of later life. Health and social care practitioners — from nursery key-workers to residential care home staff — need a clear understanding of how this dimension of development changes across the five life stages.

Infancy: Bowlby’s Attachment Theory

The most important social and emotional development in infancy is the formation of attachment — a close emotional bond between an infant and their primary caregiver. John Bowlby (1907–1990) proposed that attachment is a biological drive: infants are programmed to seek proximity to a caregiver in order to survive. His theory had several key claims that practitioners must be able to name and explain.

Bowlby argued for monotropy — the idea that infants form one primary attachment that is qualitatively different from all others. This primary figure (usually, but not always, the mother) provides the infant with an internal working model: a mental template of what relationships are like, which shapes expectations of all future relationships. Bowlby also proposed a critical period of approximately 0–3 years, within which a secure attachment must form or the individual will suffer lasting developmental harm.

Key Fact

Bowlby’s 44 Thieves Study (1944) compared 44 juvenile thieves with a control group. He found that 14 of the thieves displayed “affectionless psychopathy” — a lack of concern for others — and that a significant proportion of these had experienced maternal deprivation (disruption to the primary attachment) in early childhood. Bowlby used this as evidence that broken attachment bonds in the critical period cause lasting emotional and social damage.

Ainsworth’s Strange Situation

Mary Ainsworth (1913–1999) wanted to study how the quality of the attachment bond varied between infants. She designed the Strange Situation (1970) — a controlled laboratory procedure in which an infant is placed in a series of brief scenarios involving a caregiver and a stranger. Ainsworth observed the infant’s behaviour during separation from the caregiver and, crucially, during reunion.

Ainsworth identified three main attachment types from her observations:

Secure attachment (approximately 70% of Ainsworth’s sample): The infant is upset when the caregiver leaves but is easily comforted on return and quickly returns to exploring. This reflects consistent, sensitive caregiving. Securely attached infants develop positive internal working models — they tend to form trusting relationships later in life.

Insecure-avoidant attachment (approximately 20%): The infant shows little distress when the caregiver leaves and appears to ignore them on return. This reflects caregiving that has consistently rejected or ignored the infant’s emotional signals. These infants have learned to suppress attachment-seeking behaviours.

Insecure-resistant (ambivalent) attachment (approximately 10%): The infant is highly distressed when the caregiver leaves and cannot be easily comforted on return — pushing the caregiver away while also seeking closeness. This reflects inconsistent caregiving, where the caregiver sometimes responds sensitively and sometimes does not. The infant is uncertain about whether the caregiver can be relied upon.

A nursery key-worker observing a child who shows little distress at parental drop-off and remains distant at pick-up may note this as a possible indicator of insecure-avoidant attachment — and may raise this with their SENCO or family support worker as part of an early-years welfare assessment.

Key Fact

Bowlby and Ainsworth are distinct contributions: Bowlby explained the existence of attachment and its importance (monotropy, critical period, 44 Thieves); Ainsworth explained how attachment quality varies between infants (secure, insecure-avoidant, insecure-resistant). Both names must be correctly matched to their contribution in exam answers.

Childhood: Self-Concept, Play, and Primary Socialisation

During childhood, children develop a growing sense of self-concept — an awareness of themselves as separate people with distinct characteristics. A young child begins to describe themselves in concrete terms (“I am tall”, “I am good at drawing”) before developing a more complex self-concept in adolescence.

Play is the primary vehicle for social development in childhood. Theorists describe stages of play moving from solitary and parallel play (young toddlers) to associative and cooperative play (older children). Primary school-aged children play in groups, negotiate rules, resolve conflicts, and build friendships based on shared interests — all important social skills practised in an informal setting before formal work relationships develop later.

Primary socialisation — the process of learning values, norms, and expectations from the family — is the dominant social influence in early childhood. As children move through school, secondary socialisation through peers, teachers, and wider society becomes increasingly important. Role models outside the family begin to shape behaviour and self-image.

Adolescence: Identity, Peer Influence, and First Intimate Relationships

Adolescence brings dramatic social and emotional changes. The central emotional task — identity formation — involves working out who you are in relation to your peers, family, culture, and aspirations. Peer groups become more influential than parents in shaping behaviour, values, and lifestyle choices.

Adolescents form their first intimate relationships outside the family. These relationships provide new emotional experiences and are formative for the internal working model of romantic partnerships. Young people also begin to assert autonomy — pushing for independence from parental control — while still depending on their families for security.

Albert Bandura’s social learning theory argues that much of human behaviour is learned through observation and modelling — watching others and imitating their behaviour, particularly when the model is admired or rewarded. Vicarious reinforcement occurs when an individual imitates a behaviour after observing someone else being rewarded for it, without being rewarded themselves. In adolescence, peer role models and social media influencers are particularly powerful models. A teenager who observes peers gaining social approval for a behaviour is more likely to imitate it — whether that behaviour is positive (volunteering, studying) or negative (smoking, risky behaviour). Social care practitioners working with young people in youth clubs or community settings use understanding of social learning to design positive role-model programmes.

Adulthood and Later Adulthood: Relationships, Loss, and Dependency

In adulthood, social networks are typically at their widest. Long-term intimate partnerships, work relationships, friendships, and parenting responsibilities form the fabric of adult social life. Parenthood in particular represents a major shift in social and emotional role — an adult becomes responsible for a new attachment relationship, reversing the direction of caregiving.

In later adulthood, the social and emotional landscape changes again. Retirement can bring a positive sense of freedom but also removes a key source of identity, purpose, and daily social contact. Bereavement of partners and close friends is more frequent, and social networks often shrink. Increased physical dependency can affect self-esteem and the emotional balance of close relationships. Loneliness is a significant and well-documented risk in this life stage — day centres, befriending services, and community groups all aim to address it within the care sector.
